skills.name: benchmarking
skills.description: Guide for building, running, and analyzing Nanvix performance benchmarks. Use this when asked about benchmark setup, execution, or interpretation.

skills.name: build
skills.description: Guide for building, formatting, linting, and spell-checking Nanvix with z. Use this when asked to build or validate the repository.

skills.name: ci-cd-pipeline
skills.description: Guide for Nanvix CI and GitHub Actions workflow behavior, including local pipeline execution and matrix coverage. Use this when asked about CI checks, workflow failures, or release flow.

skills.name: coding-standards
skills.description: Detailed Nanvix coding, documentation, and review standards across Rust, C/C++, Python, and Shell. Use this when asked to implement or review code quality conventions.

skills.name: daemon-development
skills.description: Guide for developing and debugging Nanvix daemons, including guest daemons and host linuxd behavior. Use this when asked about daemon architecture or daemon changes.

skills.name: gdb-debugging
skills.description: Guide for debugging Nanvix guests using GDB remote debugging over the microvm machine type. Use this when asked about attaching GDB, setting breakpoints, or stepping through kernel code.

skills.name: kernel-development
skills.description: Guide for modifying and debugging the Nanvix kernel architecture and kernel-call paths. Use this when asked about kernel internals or kernel implementation changes.

skills.name: library-development
skills.description: Guide for creating and modifying Nanvix libraries under src/libs, including guest no_std and host std crates. Use this when asked about library architecture or crate changes.

skills.name: test-development
skills.description: Guide for writing, running, and debugging Nanvix unit, integration, and system tests in Rust and C/C++. Use this when asked about test implementation or failures.

skills.name: test
skills.description: Guide for running Nanvix tests with z. Use this when asked to run unit tests, integration tests, or the full test suite.

skills.name: troubleshooting
skills.description: Guide for diagnosing Nanvix build, runtime, and test failures, including cleanup and debugging workflows. Use this when asked to investigate errors or unstable behavior.

skills.name: user-app-development
skills.description: Guide for developing, building, and running Nanvix user-space applications across supported runtimes and languages. Use this when asked about guest app implementation or execution.

result.content:
1. # View Design: `mm::phys::frame`
2. 
3. > Status: the View for this module **already exists** in the codebase and is on
4. > the do-not-modify list (`FrameAllocView` + `FrameAllocView::wf` in
5. > `mod.spec.rs`; `View for Inner` in `frame.proof.rs`; the `PhysMemView`
6. > singleton wrapper + `phys_view()` in `mod.spec.rs`). This document reconstructs
7. > the design **from the caller analysis and public signatures only**, applies the
8. > substitution test to every field, and confirms the existing design is the right
9. > one (no change required). Rejected alternatives are recorded so future
10. > reviewers can see why each field is shaped the way it is.
11. 
12. ---
13. 
14. ## Abstract Resource
15. 
16. To callers, `frame` is **the system's single global pool of physical page
17. frames**: a fixed universe of page-aligned physical addresses partitioned into
18. *allocated* vs *free*, with a per-frame *reference count* layered on top so a
19. frame can be shared (copy-on-write) and is returned to the free pool only when
20. its last reference is released. Callers reach it through `pub(super)` free
21. functions over a singleton; they never see the backing bitmap or the BSS
22. refcount array.
23. 
24. Two distinct abstraction levels appear in the caller analysis, so the design has
25. two View layers:
26. 
27. 1. **`FrameAllocView`** — the abstract reservation state of the allocator
28.    itself (what `Inner::*` methods transform).
29. 2. **`PhysMemView`** — the module-level singleton wrapper that adds the boot
30.    `initialized` lifecycle gate and is the handle every free-function shim
31.    (`alloc`, `free`, `share`, …) states its contract over (`phys_view()`).
32. 
33. ---
34. 
35. ## View Struct
36. 
37. ### Allocator view (mirrors `Inner@`)
38. 
39. ```rust
40. pub struct FrameAllocView {
41.     /// Page-aligned physical addresses currently reserved (handed out or booked).
42.     pub allocated_frames: Set<int>,
43.     /// Page-aligned physical addresses currently available for allocation.
44.     pub free_frames: Set<int>,
45.     /// Per-frame reference count. A frame is a key iff it is allocated; the
46.     /// value (1..=255) is how many owners share it. Models copy-on-write.
47.     pub refcounts: Map<int, int>,
48. }
49. ```
50. 
51. ### Singleton view (the handle shims are stated over)
52. 
53. ```rust
54. pub struct PhysMemView {
55.     /// Boot lifecycle gate: `false` before `init`, `true` after a successful
56.     /// `init`. Models "initialized-before-use"; `instance()` panics if false.
57.     pub initialized: bool,
58.     /// The global allocator's reservation state. Well-formed once initialized.
59.     pub frames: FrameAllocView,
60. }
61. ```
62. 
63. All state is expressed in **mathematical types** (`Set<int>`, `Map<int,int>`,
64. `bool`) over **physical addresses**, never machine types, bit indices, or
65. pointers. A caller who has never read the implementation can name every field:
66. "which frames are allocated", "which are free", "how many owners each allocated
67. frame has", and "has the allocator been brought up yet".
68. 
69. ---
70. 
71. ## Well-formedness Invariant
72. 
73. ```rust
74. // FrameAllocView::wf  (do-not-modify; reproduced for reference)
75. pub open spec fn wf(&self) -> bool {
76.     // Page-alignment of every tracked address.
77.     &&& forall|a: int| self.allocated_frames.contains(a) ==> a % spec_page_size() == 0
78.     &&& forall|a: int| self.free_frames.contains(a)      ==> a % spec_page_size() == 0
79.     // Allocated and free are disjoint.
80.     &&& self.allocated_frames.disjoint(self.free_frames)
81.     // Allocated <=> positive refcount.
82.     &&& forall|a: int| #[trigger] self.allocated_frames.contains(a) <==>
83.             self.refcounts.contains_key(a) && self.refcounts[a] > 0
84.     // Free frames carry no refcount entry.
85.     &&& forall|a: int| #[trigger] self.free_frames.contains(a) ==>
86.             !self.refcounts.contains_key(a)
87.     // Refcounts fit in a u8 (kernel caps sharers at MAX_PROCESSES <= 255).
88.     &&& forall|a: int| self.refcounts.contains_key(a) ==> 0 < self.refcounts[a] <= 255
89. }
90. 
91. // PhysMemView::inv  (do-not-modify)
92. pub open spec fn inv(self) -> bool {
93.     self.initialized ==> self.frames.wf()
94. }
95. ```
96. 
97. These invariants encode exactly the caller-perspective facts from the analysis:
98. the **partition** (disjoint, page-aligned), the **refcount coupling**
99. (`allocated ⟺ refcount > 0`, free frames have no entry), the **u8 bound**
100. (`0 < c ≤ 255`), and **initialized-before-use** (well-formedness is only claimed
101. once the singleton is up). No bitmap- or array-specific clause leaks into the
102. caller-facing `wf`; the implementation-coupling invariant (bitmap bit ⟺ refcount
103. slot, tail-zero, slice length) lives separately in the do-not-modify
104. `Inner::internal_inv`.
105. 
106. ---
107. 
108. ## Spec Transition Functions
109. 
110. The mutating operations are expressed as transitions on the View. Two
111. complementary forms appear, both reusing only View vocabulary:
112. 
113. **Reusable helpers on `PhysMemView`** (do-not-modify; used by `mod`/`manager`):
114. 
115. ```rust
116. impl PhysMemView {
117.     // Derived predicates (NOT fields — see Rejected Alternatives).
118.     pub open spec fn covered(self) -> Set<int> {
119.         self.frames.allocated_frames.union(self.frames.free_frames)
120.     }
121.     pub open spec fn region_frames(start: int, size: int) -> Set<int> {
122.         let first = start / spec_page_size();
123.         let last  = (start + size) / spec_page_size();
124.         set_int_range(first, last).map(|i: int| i * spec_page_size())
125.     }
126. 
127.     // State transitions.
128.     pub open spec fn spec_initialize(self, initial: FrameAllocView) -> PhysMemView {
129.         PhysMemView { initialized: true, frames: initial }
130.     }
131.     pub open spec fn spec_book_frame(self, addr: int) -> PhysMemView { /* free→alloc, rc=1 */ }
132.     pub open spec fn spec_book_frames(self, frames: Set<int>) -> PhysMemView { /* set form */ }
133. }
134. ```
135. 
136. **Inline `FrameAllocView` literals** in the `Inner::*` contracts capture the
137. per-operation post-state declaratively (each is a pure set/map rewrite):
138. 
139. | Operation | Abstract transition on `self@` |
140. |-----------|--------------------------------|
141. | `alloc` (Ok) | pick `f ∈ free_frames`; `allocated += f`, `free −= f`, `refcounts[f] = 1` |
142. | `alloc_contiguous` (Ok) | `frames = {base + i·PAGE : 0≤i<count} ⊆ free`; `allocated ∪= frames`, `free ∖= frames`, each `refcounts = 1` |
143. | `book` (Ok) | `f ∈ free`; `allocated += f`, `free −= f`, `refcounts[f] = 1` |
144. | `alloc_range` (Ok) | `region_frames ⊆ free`; bulk move as above |
145. | `share` (Ok) | `f ∈ allocated`; `refcounts[f] += 1` (sets unchanged) |
146. | `free` (Ok) | if `refcounts[f] == 1`: `allocated −= f`, `free += f`, drop key; else `refcounts[f] −= 1` |
147. | `refcount` / `is_covered` / `free_count` | pure queries; no transition |
148. 
149. Each transition rewrites only the three abstract fields; the unchanged field(s)
150. are preserved explicitly (frame condition), matching the existing contracts.
151. 
152. ---
153. 
154. ## Design Rationale (per field, with substitution test)
155. 
156. > Substitution test: *"If the implementation were completely rewritten with a
157. > different algorithm (free-list, buddy allocator, B-tree of extents…), would
158. > this field still make sense?"*
159. 
160. - **`allocated_frames: Set<int>`** — every caller of `alloc`, `alloc_contiguous`,
161.   `book`, `alloc_range`, `share`, `refcount` asserts "the frame is now / is still
162.   in `allocated_frames`". *Substitution:* any allocator must know which frames it
163.   has handed out, regardless of how it stores that fact. ✅ Survives. Addresses
164.   (not bit indices) because callers hold `FrameAddress`/`PageAligned<…>` and
165.   compare via `frame@`.
166. 
167. - **`free_frames: Set<int>`** — `alloc`/`book`/`alloc_range` require the target be
168.   *in* `free_frames`; `free_count`'s watermark gate reasons over `free_frames`
169.   (`spec_watermark_ok`, `.finite()`/`.len()`); the partition invariant needs it.
170.   *Substitution:* "which frames are available" is intrinsic to any allocator. ✅
171.   Survives.
172. 
173. - **`refcounts: Map<int, int>`** — `share` (+1), `free` (−1, release on reaching
174.   0), and `refcount` (exact value) are *defined* by this map; fresh allocations
175.   pin `refcounts[f] == 1`. Copy-on-write is the whole reason the abstraction

 # View Design: `mm::phys::frame`
 
 > Status: the View for this module **already exists** in the codebase and is on
 > the do-not-modify list (`FrameAllocView` + `FrameAllocView::wf` in
 > `mod.spec.rs`; `View for Inner` in `frame.proof.rs`; the `PhysMemView`
 > singleton wrapper + `phys_view()` in `mod.spec.rs`). This document reconstructs
 > the design **from the caller analysis and public signatures only**, applies the
 > substitution test to every field, and confirms the existing design is the right
 > one (no change required). Rejected alternatives are recorded so future
 > reviewers can see why each field is shaped the way it is.
 
 ---
 
 ## Abstract Resource
 
 To callers, `frame` is **the system's single global pool of physical page
 frames**: a fixed universe of page-aligned physical addresses partitioned into
 *allocated* vs *free*, with a per-frame *reference count* layered on top so a
 frame can be shared (copy-on-write) and is returned to the free pool only when
 its last reference is released. Callers reach it through `pub(super)` free
 functions over a singleton; they never see the backing bitmap or the BSS
 refcount array.
 
 Two distinct abstraction levels appear in the caller analysis, so the design has
 two View layers:
 
 1. **`FrameAllocView`** — the abstract reservation state of the allocator
    itself (what `Inner::*` methods transform).
 2. **`PhysMemView`** — the module-level singleton wrapper that adds the boot
    `initialized` lifecycle gate and is the handle every free-function shim
    (`alloc`, `free`, `share`, …) states its contract over (`phys_view()`).
 
 ---
 
 ## View Struct
 
 ### Allocator view (mirrors `Inner@`)
 
 ```rust
 pub struct FrameAllocView {
     /// Page-aligned physical addresses currently reserved (handed out or booked).
     pub allocated_frames: Set<int>,
     /// Page-aligned physical addresses currently available for allocation.
     pub free_frames: Set<int>,
     /// Per-frame reference count. A frame is a key iff it is allocated; the
     /// value (1..=255) is how many owners share it. Models copy-on-write.
     pub refcounts: Map<int, int>,
 }
 ```
 
 ### Singleton view (the handle shims are stated over)
 
 ```rust
 pub struct PhysMemView {
     /// Boot lifecycle gate: `false` before `init`, `true` after a successful
     /// `init`. Models "initialized-before-use"; `instance()` panics if false.
     pub initialized: bool,
     /// The global allocator's reservation state. Well-formed once initialized.
     pub frames: FrameAllocView,
 }
 ```
 
 All state is expressed in **mathematical types** (`Set<int>`, `Map<int,int>`,
 `bool`) over **physical addresses**, never machine types, bit indices, or
 pointers. A caller who has never read the implementation can name every field:
 "which frames are allocated", "which are free", "how many owners each allocated
 frame has", and "has the allocator been brought up yet".
 
 ---
 
 ## Well-formedness Invariant
 
 ```rust
 // FrameAllocView::wf  (do-not-modify; reproduced for reference)
 pub open spec fn wf(&self) -> bool {
     // Page-alignment of every tracked address.
     &&& forall|a: int| self.allocated_frames.contains(a) ==> a % spec_page_size() == 0
     &&& forall|a: int| self.free_frames.contains(a)      ==> a % spec_page_size() == 0
     // Allocated and free are disjoint.
     &&& self.allocated_frames.disjoint(self.free_frames)
     // Allocated <=> positive refcount.
     &&& forall|a: int| #[trigger] self.allocated_frames.contains(a) <==>
             self.refcounts.contains_key(a) && self.refcounts[a] > 0
     // Free frames carry no refcount entry.
     &&& forall|a: int| #[trigger] self.free_frames.contains(a) ==>
             !self.refcounts.contains_key(a)
     // Refcounts fit in a u8 (kernel caps sharers at MAX_PROCESSES <= 255).
     &&& forall|a: int| self.refcounts.contains_key(a) ==> 0 < self.refcounts[a] <= 255
 }
 
 // PhysMemView::inv  (do-not-modify)
 pub open spec fn inv(self) -> bool {
     self.initialized ==> self.frames.wf()
 }
 ```
 
 These invariants encode exactly the caller-perspective facts from the analysis:
 the **partition** (disjoint, page-aligned), the **refcount coupling**
 (`allocated ⟺ refcount > 0`, free frames have no entry), the **u8 bound**
 (`0 < c ≤ 255`), and **initialized-before-use** (well-formedness is only claimed
 once the singleton is up). No bitmap- or array-specific clause leaks into the
 caller-facing `wf`; the implementation-coupling invariant (bitmap bit ⟺ refcount
 slot, tail-zero, slice length) lives separately in the do-not-modify
 `Inner::internal_inv`.
 
 ---
 
 ## Spec Transition Functions
 
 The mutating operations are expressed as transitions on the View. Two
 complementary forms appear, both reusing only View vocabulary:
 
 **Reusable helpers on `PhysMemView`** (do-not-modify; used by `mod`/`manager`):
 
 ```rust
 impl PhysMemView {
     // Derived predicates (NOT fields — see Rejected Alternatives).
     pub open spec fn covered(self) -> Set<int> {
         self.frames.allocated_frames.union(self.frames.free_frames)
     }
     pub open spec fn region_frames(start: int, size: int) -> Set<int> {
         let first = start / spec_page_size();
         let last  = (start + size) / spec_page_size();
         set_int_range(first, last).map(|i: int| i * spec_page_size())
     }
 
     // State transitions.
     pub open spec fn spec_initialize(self, initial: FrameAllocView) -> PhysMemView {
         PhysMemView { initialized: true, frames: initial }
     }
     pub open spec fn spec_book_frame(self, addr: int) -> PhysMemView { /* free→alloc, rc=1 */ }
     pub open spec fn spec_book_frames(self, frames: Set<int>) -> PhysMemView { /* set form */ }
 }
 ```
 
 **Inline `FrameAllocView` literals** in the `Inner::*` contracts capture the
 per-operation post-state declaratively (each is a pure set/map rewrite):
 
 | Operation | Abstract transition on `self@` |
 |-----------|--------------------------------|
 | `alloc` (Ok) | pick `f ∈ free_frames`; `allocated += f`, `free −= f`, `refcounts[f] = 1` |
 | `alloc_contiguous` (Ok) | `frames = {base + i·PAGE : 0≤i<count} ⊆ free`; `allocated ∪= frames`, `free ∖= frames`, each `refcounts = 1` |
 | `book` (Ok) | `f ∈ free`; `allocated += f`, `free −= f`, `refcounts[f] = 1` |
 | `alloc_range` (Ok) | `region_frames ⊆ free`; bulk move as above |
 | `share` (Ok) | `f ∈ allocated`; `refcounts[f] += 1` (sets unchanged) |
 | `free` (Ok) | if `refcounts[f] == 1`: `allocated −= f`, `free += f`, drop key; else `refcounts[f] −= 1` |
 | `refcount` / `is_covered` / `free_count` | pure queries; no transition |
 
 Each transition rewrites only the three abstract fields; the unchanged field(s)
 are preserved explicitly (frame condition), matching the existing contracts.
 
 ---
 
 ## Design Rationale (per field, with substitution test)
 
 > Substitution test: *"If the implementation were completely rewritten with a
 > different algorithm (free-list, buddy allocator, B-tree of extents…), would
 > this field still make sense?"*
 
 - **`allocated_frames: Set<int>`** — every caller of `alloc`, `alloc_contiguous`,
   `book`, `alloc_range`, `share`, `refcount` asserts "the frame is now / is still
   in `allocated_frames`". *Substitution:* any allocator must know which frames it
   has handed out, regardless of how it stores that fact. ✅ Survives. Addresses
   (not bit indices) because callers hold `FrameAddress`/`PageAligned<…>` and
   compare via `frame@`.
 
 - **`free_frames: Set<int>`** — `alloc`/`book`/`alloc_range` require the target be
   *in* `free_frames`; `free_count`'s watermark gate reasons over `free_frames`
   (`spec_watermark_ok`, `.finite()`/`.len()`); the partition invariant needs it.
   *Substitution:* "which frames are available" is intrinsic to any allocator. ✅
   Survives.
 
 - **`refcounts: Map<int, int>`** — `share` (+1), `free` (−1, release on reaching
   0), and `refcount` (exact value) are *defined* by this map; fresh allocations
   pin `refcounts[f] == 1`. Copy-on-write is the whole reason the abstraction
   carries counts. *Substitution:* reference-counted shared ownership is a
   behavioral contract, not an implementation choice — a free-list or buddy
   rewrite still needs per-frame counts. ✅ Survives. Keyed by **address** and
   present **iff allocated**, so it doubles as the allocated-set witness via `wf`.
 
 - **`PhysMemView.initialized: bool`** — every shim except `init` requires
   `phys_view().initialized`; `instance()` panics otherwise; `free` from `Drop`
   must preserve `inv()` which is gated on this flag. *Substitution:* a one-shot
   boot gate is inherent to a process-wide singleton, independent of its internals.
   ✅ Survives.
 
 - **`PhysMemView.frames: FrameAllocView`** — composes the allocator state into the
   singleton handle the shims are specified over. *Substitution:* a singleton is
   exactly "lifecycle + the resource it guards". ✅ Survives.
 
 **Derived, not stored:** `covered()` (= `allocated ∪ free`, the abstraction of
 `is_covered`), `region_frames()` (the frame set of a region, used by `book` /
 `alloc_range`), and the free count (`free_frames.len()` under `.finite()`) are
 **methods/derivations**, never fields — they are computable from the three core
 fields, so storing them would violate minimality.
 
 ---
 
 ## Quality Review
 
 | Criterion | Verdict |
 |-----------|---------|
 | **Substitution** | Every field survives a complete allocator rewrite (sets of allocated/free addresses + refcount map + boot flag are algorithm-independent). ✅ |
 | **Caller-only** | Each field names a concept from the caller analysis (allocated/free/shared/initialized). No bitmap, slice, pointer, or bit index appears. ✅ |
 | **Complete** | All observed caller needs are expressible: alloc/book post-state, contiguity (`{base+i·PAGE}`), free/share refcount transitions, `refcount` value, `is_covered` (`covered()`), `free_count` watermark (`free_frames`), init gate. ✅ |
 | **Minimal** | Each field is used by ≥1 contract; redundant candidates (free-count, covered-universe, bit-vector) are derived or rejected. ✅ |
 | **No code-as-spec** | Transitions are set/map rewrites (`insert`/`remove`/`union`/`difference`), never bitmap scans or loop logic. WHAT, not HOW. ✅ |
 
 ---
 
 ## Rejected Alternatives
 
 - **Bitmap as `Seq<bool>` / bit-vector indexed by frame number.** Mirrors the
   concrete `Bitmap`. Fails substitution — a free-list or buddy allocator has no
   bits. Callers never reason in bits; they hold addresses. ❌
 
 - **Keying by frame *number* (bit index) instead of physical *address*.** The
   bitmap's natural key, but callers compare `frame@` (a physical address). Using
   indices would leak the `addr = i · PAGE_SIZE` indexing into every caller proof.
   Addresses keep the View in the caller's vocabulary. ❌ (The index↔address map
   `frame_addr_of` is correctly confined to `internal_inv` / the `view()` mapping,
   not the View surface.)
 
 - **A `free_count: usize`/`nat` field.** Redundant: derivable as
   `free_frames.len()` (with `free_frames.finite()`). The watermark caller reasons
   over the set directly via `spec_watermark_ok`. Storing it would add an
   invariant-coupling burden for zero new information. ❌ (Kept as a derivation.)
 
 - **A `covered: Set<int>` field.** Equal to `allocated_frames ∪ free_frames`.
   Provided as the `covered()` **method** instead, so `is_covered`'s contract reads
   naturally without a field that must be kept in sync. ❌ as a field, ✅ as a
   helper.
 
 - **Refcounts as a parallel `Set<(int,int)>` or a single aggregate total.** A
   `Map<int,int>` is the precise abstraction: per-frame lookup for `refcount`,
   pointwise `+1`/`−1` for `share`/`free`. A set of pairs loses functional-map
   ergonomics; a total can't express per-frame queries. ❌
 
 - **Refcount as `u8`/`Map<int,u8>` (machine type).** Specs should live in `int`
   to avoid overflow reasoning; the `≤ 255` bound is stated in `wf` instead. ❌
 
 - **Dropping `allocated_frames` and deriving it from `refcounts.dom()`.**
   Technically `allocated = { a : refcounts[a] > 0 }`, so the field is *derivable*.
   **Kept explicit anyway** because (a) `wf` makes the equivalence a first-class,
   trigger-friendly fact callers cite directly (`allocated_frames.contains(f)`),
   and (b) the bulk transitions (`alloc_contiguous`, `alloc_range`) read far more
   cleanly as symmetric `union`/`difference` on `allocated`/`free` than as map
   filtering. This is a deliberate, minimal redundancy pinned by the invariant —
   not implementation mirroring. ✅ keep.
 
 - **Folding `initialized` into `FrameAllocView`.** The boot gate is a property of
   the *singleton*, not of allocator reservation state; the `Inner::*` methods
   operate on an already-live allocator. Separating it into `PhysMemView` keeps
   `FrameAllocView` reusable and lets `inv()` express "well-formed once up". ❌
   (merging), ✅ (two-layer split).
 
 ---
 
 ## Notes on Boundaries (consistency with do-not-modify specs)
 
 - `view()` for `Inner` is `closed spec fn` — public so callers can write `self@`,
   closed so the bitmap↔address mapping stays hidden. ✅ matches skill guidance.
 - `FrameAllocView::wf` / `PhysMemView::inv` are `open spec fn` — caller-visible
   abstraction-level properties. ✅
 - Reusable helpers (`covered`, `region_frames`, `spec_book_frame`,
   `spec_book_frames`, `spec_initialize`) live on the **View type**, not as extra
   `pub spec fn`s on `Inner`. ✅ matches "no extra pub spec fns on the impl".

   fn` cannot read; the exec shims pin its value through their `ensures`. This is

1. # Caller Analysis: `mm::phys::frame`
2. 
3. ## Script Output
4. 
5. See: `verus-ai-logs/nanvix-phys-phys-frame/find_callers_output.md`
6. (raw output of `find_callers_lsp.py` for `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/frame.rs`).
7. 
8. Summary from the script: 19 exec functions (10 `pub(super)` / trait-pub, 9
9. private), 1 type (`Inner`). The crate (`kernel`) has no external dependents, so
10. all callers are intra-crate, inside the `mm::phys` module tree. The script's
11. "Context" column quotes a misaligned source line; every call site below was
12. re-read from the actual code and corrected.
13. 
14. ## Module Shape (validated)
15. 
16. `frame.rs` is a **module-level singleton**. There is no caller-visible struct:
17. the private `Inner` holds the `Bitmap` + `&mut [u8]` refcount table, lives in a
18. `static mut INSTANCE: MaybeUninit<Inner>`, and is reached only through the
19. private `instance()` accessor. Every `pub(super)` free function is a one-line
20. shim `instance().<method>(...)`. Callers therefore depend purely on the
21. **free-function API** and never name `Inner`, the bitmap, or the refcount array.
22. 
23. Internal call graph (private → reached only via its public shim):
24. 
25. | Public shim (`frame::*`) | Private method | Other internal callers |
26. |--------------------------|----------------|------------------------|
27. | `alloc`            | `Inner::alloc`            | — |
28. | `alloc_contiguous` | `Inner::alloc_contiguous` | calls `Inner::alloc_range` internally |
29. | `free`             | `Inner::free`             | — |
30. | `share`            | `Inner::share`            | — |
31. | `refcount`         | `Inner::refcount`         | — |
32. | `book`             | `Inner::book`             | — |
33. | `is_covered`       | `Inner::is_covered`       | — |
34. | `alloc_range`      | `Inner::alloc_range`      | — |
35. | `free_count`       | (reads `instance().bitmap`) | — |
36. | `init`             | (writes `INSTANCE`)       | — (Skip/excluded) |
37. 
38. `instance()` is the single private chokepoint (9 callers — every shim). It
39. `panic!`s if used before `init()`; callers therefore treat
40. `phys_view().initialized` as a global precondition.
41. 
42. ## Trait Obligations
43. 
44. The frame functions themselves implement no trait. But the abstract resource is
45. consumed through two `Drop` impls, which constrain `free`:
46. 
47. - Trait: `Drop for UserFrame` (`upool.rs:198`) — calls `frame::free(self.addr)`,
48.   logs on error, never panics. Expected semantics: `free` must be callable from
49.   `Drop`, i.e. **`opens_invariants none` + `no_unwind`**, take no caller-side
50.   precondition, and preserve the subsystem invariant on every path.
51. - Trait: `Drop for KernelFrame` (`kframe.rs:189`) — identical contract on
52.   `frame::free(self.base)`.
53. 
54. These two `Drop`s are why `frame::free`'s shim contract carries **no `requires`**
55. and only `ensures phys_view().inv()` under `opens_invariants none / no_unwind`.
56. 
57. ## Caller Expectations
58. 
59. ### `alloc() -> Result<FrameAddress, Error>`
60. Callers: `Upool::alloc` (`upool.rs:268`), `PhysMemoryManager::alloc_kernel_frame`
61. (`manager.rs:353`), tests (`test.rs:58,88,115,144`).
62. - Callers assume (Ok): returned frame is page-aligned (`frame.inv()`), now in
63.   `allocated_frames`, with `refcounts[frame] == 1` (fresh, single owner). They
64.   immediately wrap it in `UserFrame`/`KernelFrame` whose `inv()` re-asserts this.
65. - Callers assume (Err): nothing about a returned frame; allocator unchanged and
66.   still `initialized` + `inv()`. (`alloc_kernel_frame` only frees on a *later*
67.   wrap failure, not on `alloc` failure.)
68. - Callers don't care about: which bit index / how the bitmap chose the frame.
69. - Would break callers: dropping page-alignment, handing out an already-allocated
70.   frame, or returning a frame not in `allocated_frames`/with refcount ≠ 1.
71. 
72. ### `alloc_contiguous(count: usize) -> Result<FrameAddress, Error>`
73. Caller: `PhysMemoryManager::alloc_many_kernel_frames` (`manager.rs:426`).
74. - Precondition supplied by caller: `count > 0` (loop/capacity already checked).
75. - Callers assume (Ok): a base address such that `base + i*PAGE_SIZE`
76.   (`0 <= i < count`) are all freshly allocated, page-strided, single-ref frames.
77.   **Contiguity is load-bearing** — kernel stacks are identity-mapped and the
78.   hardware SP walks the run linearly.
79. - Callers assume (Err): allocator unchanged. The caller's own rollback
80.   (`frame::free` of each slot) assumes the run was either fully reserved or not.
81. - Don't care about: placement strategy. Would break callers: a non-contiguous or
82.   partially-reserved run on `Ok`.
83. - **Note:** the `frame::alloc_contiguous` free-function shim currently has *no*
84.   `#[verus_spec]` (only `Inner::alloc_contiguous` is specced). The caller
85.   (`alloc_many_kernel_frames`) is itself `external_body`, so it states the
86.   contiguity guarantee directly over `phys_view()` rather than via the shim.
87. 
88. ### `free_count() -> usize`

171. *free*, with a per-frame *reference count* layered on top so a frame can be

174. free functions; they never see the backing bitmap or refcount table.

621. /// Module-level singleton storage.
622. static mut INSTANCE: MaybeUninit<Inner> = MaybeUninit::uninit();
623. 
624. /// Whether the frame allocator has been initialized.
625. static INSTANCE_INIT: AtomicBool = AtomicBool::new(false);

627. /// Returns a mutable reference to the initialized singleton.
628. fn instance() -> &'static mut Inner {
629.     if unlikely(!INSTANCE_INIT.load(ORDER)) {
630.         panic!("frame allocator used before init()");
631.     }
632. 
633.     // SAFETY: `INSTANCE_INIT` is `true`, so `INSTANCE` has been fully written by `init()`.
634.     // The kernel is single-threaded with interrupts disabled, so no concurrent access is possible.
635.     unsafe { INSTANCE.assume_init_mut() }
636. }

642. /// Initialize the frame allocator singleton.
643. ///
644. /// # Safety
645. ///
646. /// Must be called exactly once during boot, before any other function
647. /// in this module.
648. #[verus_spec(result =>
649.     ensures
650.         // `init` establishes the subsystem invariant. On success the allocator is
651.         // marked initialized; on either outcome the abstract view is well-formed
652.         // (vacuously so if it never became initialized).
653.         phys_view().inv(),
654.         match result {
655.             Ok(()) => phys_view().initialized,
656.             Err(_) => true,
657.         },
658. )]
659. pub(super) unsafe fn init(bitmap: Bitmap) -> Result<(), Error> {
660.     if unlikely(INSTANCE_INIT.load(ORDER)) {
661.         return Err(Error::new(ErrorCode::InvalidArgument, "frame allocator already initialized"));
662.     }
663. 
664.     info!(
665.         "frame allocator: {} frames, {} MB",
666.         bitmap.number_of_bits(),
667.         (bitmap.number_of_bits() * mem::FRAME_SIZE) / constants::MEGABYTE,
668.     );
669. 
670.     let nframes: usize = bitmap.number_of_bits();
671.     if nframes > NFRAMES {
672.         return Err(Error::new(
673.             ErrorCode::InvalidArgument,
674.             "frame bitmap is larger than the configured refcount storage",
675.         ));
676.     }
677. 
678.     // SAFETY: single-threaded boot; no other reference to `REFCOUNT_STORAGE` exists.
679.     let refcount: &'static mut [u8] = unsafe { &mut REFCOUNT_STORAGE[..] };
680. 
681.     // Defensively sync refcounts with any bits already set in the incoming bitmap. The
682.     // current microvm boot path supplies an empty bitmap and performs all reservations
683.     // via `book()` / `alloc_range()` after `init()`, so this loop normally does nothing.
684.     // It is kept as a safety net so a future boot path that hands us a pre-populated
685.     // bitmap (for example to express firmware-reserved regions) does not silently end
686.     // up with `bitmap bit = 1, refcount = 0`, which would cause the first `free()` of
687.     // such a frame to be rejected as a spurious double-free.
688.     for (i, slot) in refcount.iter_mut().enumerate().take(nframes) {
689.         if matches!(bitmap.test(i), Ok(true)) {
690.             *slot = 1;
691.         }
692.     }
693. 
694.     // SAFETY: single-threaded boot; no other reference to `INSTANCE` exists.
695.     unsafe { INSTANCE.write(Inner { bitmap, refcount }) };
696.     INSTANCE_INIT.store(true, ORDER);
697.     Ok(())
698. }

702.     requires
703.         phys_view().initialized,
704.         phys_view().inv(),
705.     ensures

708.         // On success the returned frame is freshly reserved: page-aligned, now in

710.         // is reported about the returned (absent) frame.
711.         match result {
712.             Ok(frame) => {
713.                 &&& frame.inv()
714.                 &&& phys_view().frames.allocated_frames.contains(frame@)

792. }

3. 
4. // PhysMemoryManager - Specifications
5. //
6. // This file contains specification functions and view types.
7. 
8. verus! {
9. 
10. use crate::hal::mem::spec_page_size;
11. use vstd::map::*;
12. 
13. pub uninterp spec fn byte_at_address(ptr: int) -> u8;
14. 
15. /// Abstract view of the frame allocator (`frame::Inner`).
16. ///
17. /// Captures which physical frames are currently allocated vs. free,
18. /// together with a per-frame reference count that models shared
19. /// ownership (e.g. copy-on-write after `share()`).
20. pub struct FrameAllocView
21. {
22.     pub allocated_frames: Set<int>,
23.     pub free_frames: Set<int>,
24.     /// Maps each allocated frame address to its reference count.
25.     /// A frame is present in the map iff it is currently allocated.
26.     pub refcounts: Map<int, int>,
27. }
28. 
29. impl FrameAllocView
30. {
31.     pub open spec fn wf(&self) -> bool
32.     {
33.         // Page-alignment
34.         &&& forall|addr: int| self.allocated_frames.contains(addr) ==> addr % spec_page_size() == 0
35.         &&& forall|addr: int| self.free_frames.contains(addr) ==> addr % spec_page_size() == 0
36.         // Disjoint
37.         &&& self.allocated_frames.disjoint(self.free_frames)
38.         // Allocated ↔ refcount consistency: a frame is allocated iff it has a positive refcount
39.         &&& forall|addr: int| #[trigger] self.allocated_frames.contains(addr) <==>
40.             self.refcounts.contains_key(addr) && self.refcounts[addr] > 0
41.         // Free frames have no refcount entry
42.         &&& forall|addr: int| #[trigger] self.free_frames.contains(addr) ==>
43.             !self.refcounts.contains_key(addr)
44.         // Refcount bounded by u8 range
45.         &&& forall|addr: int| self.refcounts.contains_key(addr) ==>
46.             0 < self.refcounts[addr] <= 255
47.     }
48. }
49. 
50. } // end verus!
51. 
52. //==================================================================================================
53. // std `LinkedList` type specification
54. //==================================================================================================
55. //
56. // vstd does not provide a specification for `alloc::collections::LinkedList`. Verified functions in
57. // this module (`init`) take `LinkedList` parameters, so Verus needs to know the type. We declare it
58. // as an opaque external type. We deliberately do NOT provide a `View`/iterator specification: doing
59. // so requires implementing vstd's `View`/`ForLoopGhostIterator` traits for the foreign std types
60. // `LinkedList`/`Iter`, which the Rust orphan rule forbids from a downstream crate (E0117), and the
61. // pinned `vstd` dependency cannot be extended. Consequently the `for region in list.iter()` loops in
62. // `book_physical_memory_regions` / `book_mmio_regions` cannot be body-verified here; those two
63. // functions are marked `external_body` (see `verus-unsupported.md`).
64. 
65. verus! {
66. 
67. use core::alloc::Allocator;
68. 
69. #[verifier::external_type_specification]
70. #[verifier::external_body]
71. #[verifier::reject_recursive_types(T)]
72. #[verifier::reject_recursive_types(A)]
73. pub struct ExLinkedList<T, A: Allocator>(LinkedList<T, A>);
74. 
75. } // end verus!
76. 
77. //==================================================================================================
78. // `mm::phys` boot-subsystem View
79. //==================================================================================================
80. 
81. verus! {
82. 
83. use vstd::set_lib::set_int_range;
84. 
85. /// Abstract state of the global physical-memory subsystem managed by `mm::phys`.
86. ///
87. /// Models the boot lifecycle of the frame-allocator singleton plus its
88. /// frame-reservation state. The `frames` component mirrors `frame::instance()@`;
89. /// the `initialized` flag mirrors the `INSTANCE_INIT` lifecycle gate.
90. pub struct PhysMemView {
91.     /// Whether the frame-allocator singleton has been established
92.     /// (i.e. `init` ran once and returned `Ok`). Models one-shot/monotonic
93.     /// boot: `false` before `init`, `true` after a successful `init`.
94.     pub initialized: bool,
95.     /// Abstract reservation state of the global frame allocator: which physical
96.     /// frames are reserved (allocated) vs. free, with per-frame refcounts.
97.     /// Meaningful (well-formed) only once `initialized` is `true`.
98.     pub frames: FrameAllocView,
99. }
100. 
101. impl PhysMemView {
102.     /// Well-formedness: once the allocator is established, the frame-allocator
103.     /// invariant holds. Before initialization there is no allocator, so no
104.     /// constraint applies.
105.     pub open spec fn inv(self) -> bool {
106.         self.initialized ==> self.frames.wf()
107.     }
108. 
109.     /// Frames the allocator actually tracks (covered by the bitmap): the union
110.     /// of reserved and free frames. The abstract form of `is_covered`.
111.     pub open spec fn covered(self) -> Set<int> {
112.         self.frames.allocated_frames.union(self.frames.free_frames)
113.     }
114. 
115.     /// The set of frame addresses occupied by a region `[start, start+size)`.
116.     pub open spec fn region_frames(start: int, size: int) -> Set<int> {
117.         let first = start / spec_page_size();
118.         let last = (start + size) / spec_page_size();
119.         set_int_range(first, last).map(|i: int| i * spec_page_size())
120.     }
121. 
122.     /// `init` established the allocator from the caller-supplied bitmap state;
123.     /// lifecycle flips on.
124.     pub open spec fn spec_initialize(self, initial: FrameAllocView) -> PhysMemView {
125.         PhysMemView { initialized: true, frames: initial }
126.     }
127. 
128.     /// Book one covered frame: move `addr` from free to allocated, refcount = 1.
129.     /// Mirrors `Inner::book`'s `Ok` post-state.
130.     pub open spec fn spec_book_frame(self, addr: int) -> PhysMemView {
131.         PhysMemView {
132.             frames: FrameAllocView {
133.                 allocated_frames: self.frames.allocated_frames.insert(addr),
134.                 free_frames: self.frames.free_frames.remove(addr),
135.                 refcounts: self.frames.refcounts.insert(addr, 1int),
136.             },
137.             ..self
138.         }
139.     }
140. 
141.     /// Book a set of frames at once: move them all from free to allocated, each
142.     /// with refcount = 1. Mirrors `Inner::alloc_range`'s `Ok` post-state and
143.     /// generalizes it from a contiguous region to an arbitrary frame set.
144.     pub open spec fn spec_book_frames(self, frames: Set<int>) -> PhysMemView {
145.         PhysMemView {
146.             frames: FrameAllocView {
147.                 allocated_frames: self.frames.allocated_frames.union(frames),
148.                 free_frames: self.frames.free_frames.difference(frames),
149.                 refcounts: self.frames.refcounts.union_prefer_right(
150.                     Map::new(|a: int| frames.contains(a), |a: int| 1int),
151.                 ),
152.             },
153.             ..self
154.         }
155.     }
156. }
157. 
158. /// Abstract view of the global physical-memory subsystem at the current program
159. /// point.
160. ///
161. /// The subsystem state lives in module-level `static`s (`frame::INSTANCE` /
162. /// `frame::INSTANCE_INIT`) that a Verus `spec fn` cannot read directly, so this
163. /// is an *uninterpreted* function: the exec wrappers in `frame.rs` and the
164. /// `book_*`/`init` functions pin down its value through their `ensures` clauses.
165. /// `initialized` mirrors `INSTANCE_INIT`; `frames` mirrors `frame::instance()@`.
166. ///
167. /// This is the handle the caller-facing contract of `init` is stated over: after
168. /// a successful `init`, `phys_view().initialized` and `phys_view().inv()` hold, so
169. /// every later `frame::*` / `PhysMemoryManager::*` operation may rely on the
170. /// frame-allocator invariant.
171. pub uninterp spec fn phys_view() -> PhysMemView;
172. 
173. } // end verus!
174. 
175.

'm looking at how the shim functions like

call to `instance()`, but there's no specification linking the instance state to the physical
view where the ensures clause checks for allocated frames. I need to understand how this
verification currently works despite that apparent gap.
The
core issue is that `phys_view()` is uninterpreted and fixed, but calling `instance().alloc()` mutates the underlying state. For the postc
ondition to hold, the returned reference's view would need to equal `phys_view()` at the
post-state, yet `phys_view()` is a static function that can't distinguish between pre and post states.
This seems like a fundamental modeling problem—I need to figure out how to tie the instance
reference's view to the physical view in a way that accounts for state changes.

- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/mod.rs::book_physical_memory_regions` — iterates a std

  toolchain's `vstd` (`/mnt/toolchain/verus/vstd`) ships ghost-iterator specs only
  for `slice`/`vec`/`VecDeque`/`BTree*`/`Hash*` iterators, **not** `LinkedList`, and
  the orphan rule forbids supplying `View`/`ForLoopGhostIterator` impls for the
  foreign `linked_list::Iter` from the `kernel` crate (E0117). Genuine Verus
  front-end limitation, not a proof gap or code bug — full analysis in
  `verus-unsupported.md`. The abstract booking effect is specified over
  `PhysMemView` and discharged (no `admit`) by
  `lemma_book_region_reserves_region_frames` in `mod.proof.rs`. `ensures` keeps the
  caller-relevant guarantee: allocator stays initialized and well-formed.
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/mod.rs::book_mmio_regions` — same std-`LinkedList`
  iteration limitation as above. Abstract effect (skip-if-not-covered; book tracked
  frames) discharged by `lemma_book_mmio_skip_untracked` /
  `lemma_book_mmio_books_tracked`. `ensures` keeps allocator initialized and
  well-formed across booking.

  the abstract `bump_view`.

  `alloc` and re-materializes the slot as `&'static mut MaybeUninit<T>`; same rationale.
  `ensures` adds the `size_of::<T>()`/`align_of::<T>()` vs `(N, A)` guard arms.

## Skip / exclude from current proof target

- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/manager.rs::PhysMemoryManager::get_mut`
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/frame.rs::init`

## Allowed `external_body` — `frame::*` free-function shims (`frame.rs`)

The module-level `frame::*` free functions bridge the global allocator singleton
(`static mut INSTANCE`, reached via `instance()`) to the do-not-modify abstract
`phys_view()` / `FrameAllocView`. That bridge is a trust boundary identical in
character to the already-trusted `frame::book` / `frame::is_covered` /
`frame::alloc_range` shims: `phys_view()` is a zero-argument uninterpreted spec
function whose value cannot be tied to the `unsafe { INSTANCE.assume_init_mut() }`
static by any verifiable means. Each is `external_body` with a `#[verus_spec]`
contract stated over `phys_view()` and the returned frame values (monotone
post-state facts; there is no `old(phys_view())`). They were left unspecced when
`frame.rs` was the proof target because their sole consumer is `mm::phys::upool`;
they are specced here so `upool` can rely on them, and will be removed when the
frame singleton bridge is itself verified.

- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/frame.rs::alloc` — draws a fresh frame from the global
  allocator. `ensures` (on success) page alignment, membership in
  `allocated_frames`, and refcount = 1.
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/frame.rs::free` — releases one reference (last reference
  returns the frame to the free pool). Runs on `Drop`, so it has no precondition;
  `ensures` keeps the subsystem invariant on every path.
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/frame.rs::share` — adds a reference to an allocated
  frame. `ensures` (on success) the frame stays allocated / refcounted.
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/frame.rs::refcount` — pure query of an allocated frame's
  reference count. `ensures` (on success) the returned count equals the frame's
  refcount; (on failure) the frame is not allocated.

## Allowed `external_body` — `UserFrame::drop` (`upool.rs`)

`UserFrame::drop` releases the frame's reference by calling `frame::free` and, on
the error path, logs via the `error!` macro. The `error!`/`write!` expansion uses
`core::fmt` Debug formatting (`{:?}`), which Verus cannot translate to VIR
("Unsupported constant type"). The function is therefore `external_body`; its
`#[verus_spec]` contract is honored by trusting that body. The contract is not a
new guarantee — `ensures phys_view().inv()` is exactly the post-state already
established by the `external_body` `frame::free` shim it calls, and the logging
branch performs no state change. `opens_invariants none` / `no_unwind` record that
`drop` opens no invariant and cannot unwind (errors are logged, not propagated).

- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/upool.rs::<UserFrame as Drop>::drop` — releases one
  reference on scope exit. `ensures phys_view().inv()` on every path.

`KernelFrame::new` is the first verified (`#[verus_spec]`) exec body in the proof
target that calls cross-module address-conversion / mapping helpers. Those helpers
live in `hal::mem` and `mm::virt`, which are **not yet verified**, so they are

# Build Nanvix

Use this skill when the user asks to build, compile, format, lint, or spell-check Nanvix. This
covers all build-system operations exposed through the `z` utility.

## Prerequisites

- Development environment set up per `doc/setup.md`.
- A local cross-compilation toolchain (`toolchain/`).
- **Windows 11:** GNU Make on PATH, Windows Hypervisor Platform enabled,
  Developer Mode enabled, and Rust toolchain installed. See `doc/setup.md` for details.

## Windows Setup Summary

Before building on Windows, ensure:

1. **Windows Hypervisor Platform** is enabled (`Enable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName HypervisorPlatform -All`, then reboot).
2. **Developer Mode** is on (Settings > Privacy & Security > For developers).
3. **GNU Make** is on PATH (`winget install ezwinports.make`).
4. **Rust toolchain** is installed via `winget install Rustlang.Rustup`.
5. Repository was cloned with `git clone -c core.symlinks=true`.
6. Git hooks are installed: `./z.ps1 setup`.

## Building

### Preferred Build Commands (using `z` utility)

```bash
# Build everything with the local toolchain.
./z build -- all
```

### Building Individual Components

```bash
# Kernel only.
./z build -- kernel
# Nanvixd only.
./z build -- all-nanvixd
# UserVM only.
./z build -- all-uservm
```

### Build Parameters

Set these as environment variables or pass them after `--` in the `z` command:

| Parameter        | Values                   | Default         |
|------------------|--------------------------|-----------------|
| `MACHINE`        | `microvm`                | `microvm`       |
| `TARGET`         | `x86`                    | `x86`           |
| `RELEASE`        | `yes`, `no`              | `no`            |
| `LOG_LEVEL`      | `trace`, `debug`,        | `error`         |
|                  | `info`, `warn`,          |                 |
|                  | `error`, `panic`         |                 |
| `PROFILER`       | `yes`, `no`              | `no`            |
| `DEPLOYMENT_MODE`| `standalone`,            | `standalone`    |
|                  | `single-process`,        |                 |
|                  | `multi-process`, `l2`    |                 |

Example with custom parameters:

```bash
./z build -- all RELEASE=yes LOG_LEVEL=error
```

### Manual Build Variants

```bash
# Default debug build.
./z build -- all
# Release build.
./z build -- all RELEASE=yes LOG_LEVEL=panic
# For echo-breakdown benchmark.
./z build -- all RELEASE=yes LOG_LEVEL=panic TIMESTAMP_MSG=yes
```

### Building on Windows (using `z.ps1`)

On Windows 11, the `z.ps1` PowerShell script provides the same CLI interface. Guest components are
cross-compiled using a local toolchain; host binaries (`nanvixd`, `uservm`) are built natively with the
microvm backend (WHP on Windows).

```powershell
# Build everything (guest via make + host binaries natively).
.\z.ps1 build -- all

# Build only the UserVM (native Windows build).
.\z.ps1 build -- uservm

# Build only nanvixd (native Windows build).
.\z.ps1 build -- nanvixd

# Build only nanvix-bench (native Windows build).
.\z.ps1 build -- nanvix-bench

# Build only guest components (kernel + hello-rust-nostd).
.\z.ps1 build -- guest

# Release build.
.\z.ps1 build -- all RELEASE=yes
```

Any unrecognized target is forwarded to `make`, just like on Linux:

```powershell
.\z.ps1 build -- kernel
.\z.ps1 build -- format-check
.\z.ps1 build -- lint-check
```

## Code Quality

### Formatting

```bash
# Check formatting issues.
./z build -- format-check
# Auto-fix formatting issues.
./z build -- format
```

### Linting

```bash
# Check linting issues.
./z build -- lint-check
# Auto-fix linting issues.
./z build -- lint
```

### Spell Checking

```bash
# Check spelling errors.
./z build -- spellcheck
# Fix spelling errors.
./z build -- spellcheck-fix
```

## Formal Verification

Nanvix uses Verus for formal verification of selected kernel crates. The expected Verus version is pinned in `build/verus-version`. Verification requires `VERUS_EXECUTABLE_DIR` to be set; when unset, `make verify` is a no-op.

```bash
# Install verus and run verification.
./scripts/setup/verus.sh ~/toolchain/verus
./z build -- verify VERUS_EXECUTABLE_DIR=~/toolchain/verus

# Verify a single crate.
./z build -- verify-bitmap VERUS_EXECUTABLE_DIR=~/toolchain/verus
```

- Set `VERUS_EXECUTABLE_DIR` to the directory containing the `verus` binary.
- Use `scripts/setup/verus.sh <dir>` to download the pinned release.
- The `vstd` crate version in `Cargo.toml` is exact-pinned (`=`) to match the Verus binary.

## Cleaning

```bash
./z clean        # Clean build artifacts.
./z distclean    # Remove all generated files.
```

### Cleaning on Windows

```powershell
.\z.ps1 clean        # Quick clean (UserVM artifacts + cache).
.\z.ps1 distclean    # Full clean (cargo clean + all artifacts).
```

## CI/CD Pipeline

```bash
# Run the full CI pipeline locally.
./scripts/pipeline.sh
```

The pipeline covers: spell checking, formatting, linting, building, and testing across multiple
machine and deployment configurations.

## IDE Setup (Optional)

### Visual Studio Code

Use the host-specific settings template. The Linux template invokes `./z`, while the Windows
template routes Rust Analyzer through `./z.bat build -- check`, which runs native `cargo check`
on host crates (`uservm`, `nanvixd`, `nanvix-test`, `mkramfs`).

**Linux:**

```bash
mkdir -p .vscode && cd .vscode
ln -s ../scripts/setup/vscode/settings-linux.json settings.json
```

**Windows (PowerShell):**

```powershell
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path .vscode -Force
Copy-Item scripts\setup\vscode\settings-windows.json .vscode\settings.json
```

> **Note:** The `check` target in `z.ps1` only checks host crates natively. Guest and kernel
> crates require the cross-compilation toolchain. Run
> `.\z.ps1 build -- check-kernel check-guest-binaries` for a full cross-target check.

## Troubleshooting Build Issues

- If builds fail with toolchain errors, verify `toolchain/` symlink points to a valid toolchain.
- Use `./z help` for usage information.
- **Windows:** Use `.\z.ps1 help` for Windows-specific usage information.
- **Windows:** If the UserVM build fails, verify that the Windows Hypervisor Platform feature is
  enabled (`Get-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName HypervisorPlatform`).

data.deltaContent: The
issue is that `init` is marked with `#[verus_spec]` but lacks the `external_body` attribute, even
though it's listed in tcb-allowed.md as something to skip or exclude from the current proof target. The verifier is attempting
to verify the function body when it shouldn't be, since `init` references static mutable state that shouldn
't be part of the verification scope.
The
shims already have specs but the module won't compile because `init` uses `
static mut`. The real issue is that `instance()` does unsafe static access and can't be verified, so it needs to be `
external_body` — but it's not listed in tcb-allowed.md, which creates a constraint
violation with the hard rule about only marking functions external_body if they're in the allowed
list.
So

# Spec Design Guide

## Part 1: Spec Quality Principles

### Qualities of a Good Spec

1. **Bound to exec code** — every property must appear as `requires`,
   `ensures`, or loop `invariant` on an exec function. Standalone spec
   functions that no exec function references prove nothing.
2. **Annotates the original** — specs are added directly to the original
   exec function using `#[verus_spec]` (see `verus-syntax` skill). Never
   copy exec functions into a `verus!{}` block and spec the copy — that
   verifies the copy, not the real code.
3. **Sufficient to reject bugs** — if you can imagine a buggy implementation
   that still satisfies the spec, the spec is incomplete. A sorting spec
   that omits `is_sorted` passes a function that just copies the input.
4. **Declarative, not operational** — a spec describes **what** must be true,
   not **how** the code achieves it. If you could swap quicksort for
   bubblesort and the spec still makes sense, it's a good spec.
5. **Simpler than the code** — the spec should be at a higher level of
   abstraction than the implementation. For example, where the code has
   loops, the spec may use `forall`, `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` operations, or
   recursive spec functions.
6. **Independent from the code** — two independent statements of the same truth.
   If derived by reading code line-by-line, it will reproduce bugs. A useful
   test: **could you have written this spec from just the function signature,
   type definitions, and module purpose — without reading the implementation?**
   If not, the spec likely mirrors the code rather than abstracting over it.
7. **Uses mathematical objects where they simplify reasoning** — prefer `int`
   over `u32`/`i32` (avoids overflow in specs), `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` over
   `Vec`/`HashMap`. Use `view()` / `self@` for abstract state. For pointer
   addresses, prefer `usize` over `int` — addresses are inherently
   non-negative and bounded by the address space.
8. **Written for the caller** — for each ensures clause, simulate
   writing a caller's proof that uses this function. Would you use
   this fact as-is, or would you need to transform, combine, or
   unwrap it first? A good ensures clause is one the caller writes
   directly into their proof. Prefer vstd's existing spec functions
   (e.g., `self@.contains(x)`) over manual encodings (e.g.,
   `exists|i| ... && self@[i] == x`) — callers already reason with
   vstd APIs. On `exists`: valid when it genuinely hides
   implementation choice, but if the witness is computable from inputs
   and return values through the module's public spec interface,
   `exists` hides nothing — prefer a deterministic `let` binding.

### Exec Binding Rules — Desk Reject Criteria

If exec functions have no `requires`/`ensures`, the result is a **desk reject**:
nothing was verified, regardless of how many spec functions or lemmas exist in
spec.rs/proof.rs. Our goal is a **verified implementation**, not a verified
design model.

1. **Every exec function in scope gets contracts** — "in scope" is determined
   by the verification task (e.g., caller analysis, human directive, or
   module-level verification). If scope is unclear, default to all public
   and safety-critical functions. No annotation is a desk reject; partial
   annotation beats no annotation.
2. **Search vstd before writing `assume_specification`** — vstd already
   provides specs for many std library functions. Only write
   `assume_specification` for std library or third-party dependency
   functions that vstd does not cover. Never for workspace-internal code.
   Always search vstd first.
3. **Reuse dependency specs** — before calling a function from another
   module in the project, search for its `.spec.rs`:
   `find . -name "*.spec.rs" | head -20`. If the dependency has verified
   specs, import and use them directly. If it does not, add `#[verus_spec]`
   annotations on the dependency function — do NOT use `assume_specification`
   for project-internal code (any crate in the workspace). `assume_specification`
   is only for third-party dependencies and std library functions not covered
   by vstd.
   **Why this works without `admit()`**: `--verify-module M` only verifies
   functions in module M. Specs on functions in other modules are treated as
   trusted contracts — their bodies are not checked. When those modules are
   verified later, the specs become fully proven.
5. **No floating specs** — every spec function and lemma must ultimately
   connect to an exec contract. Orphan specs are dead code.
6. **No `external_body` on current module** — the current module's functions
   must never be marked `external_body`. Use `admit()` in proof bodies to
   make Verus pass.
   **Dependency functions** in other modules may be marked `external_body`
   with `requires`/`ensures` to provide contracts that the current module
   can rely on. These are removed when the dependency module is verified.

### Anti-Patterns (reject or remove)

1. **Exec Code Mutation** — modifying existing exec code, APIs, or
   struct definitions to accommodate specs. Do not change function
   signatures, alter control flow, or add exec fields to structs.
   Adding `Ghost<T>` / `Tracked<T>` fields is allowed — they are
   erased at compile time and do not change exec behavior. However,
   prefer keeping ghost state in spec.rs (e.g., on the View type)
   rather than adding fields to exec structs; only add when the proof
   genuinely requires ghost state to flow through exec code.
   
   Exec code must NOT be changed — the code has been pre-refactored to be
   fully Verus-compatible. See `verus-constraints` skill.
2. **Verification Escape** — using `assume`, `admit`,
   or `exec_allows_no_decreases_clause` to bypass verification. Fix the
   spec or proof instead.
   
   **Exceptions (legitimate trust boundaries):**
   - `assume_specification`: for std library / external functions whose
     source code is outside the verification scope (e.g., not in our
     crate). Write the spec to match the original API documentation.

   1. **Read the official docs first**: find the function's doc comments
      in `~/.rustup/toolchains/*/lib/rustlib/src/rust/library/` using
      `grep -rn "fn <name>"`. Write the spec from these docs, not from
      reading the implementation or copying an internal helper's spec.
      Capture all documented semantics, including implicit type
      requirements (e.g., trait bounds imply properties like total ordering).
   2. **Documentation fidelity**: every ensures clause must be explicitly
      guaranteed by the original API documentation. If the doc does not
      guarantee it, mark the clause as "assumed beyond documentation".
      Conversely, every documented precondition must appear as a `requires`
      clause — omitting a precondition makes the spec unsound because
      callers will not check it.
   3. **Soft contract coverage**: identify semantic contracts that the
      compiler does not enforce but the API requires. Express these
      explicitly in the spec.
   4. **No stronger than the API**: the spec must not assume more than
      the API guarantees. Ask: "if I only read the doc (not the source
      code), would I believe this ensures clause is guaranteed?"

      assumption was checked against.

     a temporary contract placeholder (removed when that module is verified),
     and on functions pre-approved in the TCB allowed list.

     verification.

   See the audit checklist above when writing `assume_specification`.

   the loop's progress and preservation properties. A function with
   loops but no loop invariants has an incomplete spec. Verus will reject
   it. For complex invariants, define a `spec fn` predicate in spec.rs
   or proof.rs and reference it in the `invariant` clause. The invariant

   implies the function's `ensures`. The invariant may need to be
   strengthened later — that is expected.

   or describing computation step-by-step. Bad: recursive quicksort in

   ```

   ```
   self@ == ViewType { field_c: new_value, ..old(self)@ }
   ```

   inline or via spec transition functions.

   `result.is_err() ==> ...` as separate ensures clauses instead of a
   single `match`. The `match` form is complete by construction and

   Bad:
   ```
   ensures

       result.is_err() ==> self@ == old(self)@,

   self@.field_b == old(self)@.field_b,
   self@.field_c == new_value,

   ```

   ```
   self@ == ViewType { field_c: new_value, ..old(self)@ }
   ```

   inline or via spec transition functions.

       result.is_err() ==> self@ == old(self)@,
   ```

   ```

with the same rigor as the success path.

1. **State Preservation** — on error, the state must not change.
2. **Bidirectional Failure Condition** — express error conditions as abstract

   code checks. Ask: what condition at the interface level makes success
   impossible?

   not spuriously return `None`/`Err`). A spec that *allows* failure

   rely on it. Use `match` on the return value to specify both arms:

       Ok(v)  => /* success postcondition */,
       Err(e) => /* error postcondition */,

   ```

**Completely skip** (no spec needed at all):
- **Type-system guarantees** — ownership, borrow rules, type matching
- **Display/formatting** — debug output, logging, string representation
- **Boilerplate trait impls** — derived traits, mechanical delegations

**Basic ensures only** (no additional spec design):
- **Trivial accessors** — field getters still need
  `ensures result == self@.field` for callers to reason about, but
  warrant no further properties.
- **Pure wrappers** — functions that directly delegate to a single
  verified function with no additional logic.

### Property Coverage Checklist

When writing specs, systematically cover these four dimensions for each
function and type. This ensures no important properties are missed.

1. **Functional Correctness** — What does the code achieve?
   - Preconditions (requires): what must the caller guarantee?
   - Success postconditions (ensures, Ok case): new abstract state, return value, frame condition
   - Error postconditions (ensures, Err case): state preservation, failure condition in abstract terms

, deferring the actual proof to a later phase.

### Post-Generation Spec Refinement

After writing ensures clauses, review each one through the caller's eyes.

find every ensures clause natural and directly useful?**

## Part 2: Spec Classification

Specifications fall into three categories with different ownership:

### Internal

Specs that exist solely to help the verifier: helper lemmas, loop
invariants, intermediate assertions, proof-function pre/postconditions.

correctness is whether the code above can use them — the verifier
provides direct feedback.

Public function `requires`/`ensures`, type invariants exposed to
callers, View types. These define **what the module promises**.

Assumptions about layers below the verification scope: std library
behavior, hardware semantics, runtime correctness, compiler fidelity.
These are unverified: if they do not match reality, downstream proofs
may be unsound. Mechanisms include `assume_specification`,
`external_body`, and `axiom`. Which functions belong in this category
is pre-determined by the TCB allowed list — do not make new trust
boundary decisions during specification or proving.

## Part 3: View Abstraction Design

The View type and a skeletal `inv()` should already be designed before writing
specifications. Refine and extend `inv()` as you write specs — new constraints
often emerge from requires/ensures. This section summarizes the key principles
for reference.

1. **Only caller-visible state** — hide internal bookkeeping. Test: if you
   swapped the underlying data structure, would the View fields still make sense?
2. **Use abstract types** — `int` instead of `i32`, `Seq<int>` instead of
   `Vec<u64>`, `Map<K, V>` instead of `HashMap<K, V>`.
3. **`view()` is `pub closed spec fn`** — public so callers can invoke it,
   closed so implementation details don't leak.
4. **`inv()` is `pub open spec fn`** — includes `internal_inv()` plus
   abstraction-level properties (e.g., `self@.len() < usize::MAX`).

### Spec Transition Functions

For each state-mutating exec function, define a corresponding spec function
on the View type. Use `..self` to implicitly preserve unchanged fields
(frame condition):

```rust

    pub open spec fn spec_insert(self, elem: int) -> FooView {
        FooView { elements: self.elements.insert(elem), ..self }

spec transition already captures the complete state change.

`forall|i: int| i != changed_idx ==> new@[i] == old@[i]`

dynamic information (external input, hardware state, concurrent
operations) that no amount of static reasoning can discharge. A
`requires` clause here would be unsound or unusable.

find every ensures clause natural and directly useful?**

   clauses already imply? Remove anything derivable from the rest.

   proof, or must they transform it first? If the latter, provide the
   form the caller actually needs.

## Part 2: Spec Classification

Specifications fall into three categories with different ownership:

name: verification-order
description: "Determine function-level verification order within a module using the verification plan. Use at the start of proving to know which function to verify first and how to sequence work."

# Verification Order

## Purpose

When proving a module, you must verify functions in **dependency order**:
verify callees before callers. This avoids wasting effort on callers whose
callees don't yet have specs, and ensures each function's dependencies are
already proven when you reach it.

## How to Get the Order

A pre-generated verification plan may exist at:

```
{logs_dir}/verification-plan.json
```

If this file exists, use `show_fn_order.py` to display the function order:

```bash
# Show function order for a specific module
python3 {scripts_dir}/show_fn_order.py {logs_dir}/verification-plan.json \
    -m "kernel::mm::phys::kpool"

# Glob pattern to match multiple modules
python3 {scripts_dir}/show_fn_order.py {logs_dir}/verification-plan.json \
    -m "bitmap::*"
```

If the file does not exist, skip this step and use your best judgment for
function ordering (generally: leaf helpers first, public API functions last).

## How to Use the Order

1. **At the start of proving**, check for the plan and run `show_fn_order.py`.
2. **Verify functions in the listed order** (top to bottom = leaves first).
   The first function has no intra-module dependencies; later functions
   may call earlier ones.
3. **Do not skip ahead.** Resolve each function's `admit()` before moving
   to the next. This mirrors the proving-guide's "one function at a time"
   rule but with a concrete ordering.
4. **Cross-module deps** listed in the output tell you which dependency
   modules need specs. If a callee in another module lacks a spec, write
   an `assume_specification` or verify that module first.

## Output Format

```
## kernel::mm::phys::kpool
   crate: kernel  |  file: src/kernel/src/mm/phys/kpool.rs

    #  Function                        Line  In-module deps
  ───  ──────────────────────────────  ─────  ──────────────────────────────
    1  KpoolInner::alloc               L56   —
    2  KernelFrame::deref_mut          L160  —
    3  KernelFrame::clear              L144  KernelFrame::deref_mut
    4  Kpool::alloc                    L205  KpoolInner::alloc, clear
```

Use `-v` to also see cross-module dependency modules.

Functions are ordered so that by the time you reach function N, all its
intra-module dependencies (functions 1..N-1) are already verified.

code still runs normally, and type-checking passes. This is allowed since adding

data.deltaContent: I
'm running into translation blockers in the EXEC method bodies—things like `debug_assert_eq!
`, the `FrameNumber` type, `FrameAddress::from_frame_number`, and the `error!` macro all rely on external types
and functions that Verus can't verify without proper specifications. These are genuine obstacles to
body-verification without adding specs for all these dependencies.
The reality
is that the Inner methods need to stay as `external_body` because they're full of unsupported constructs like
`error!` and `debug_assert!` macros (which expand to `core::fmt::Arguments`) and architecture
-specific types. This matches the original state before the strip, and it's the same justification already documented
for `UserFrame::drop`. The strip was too aggressive—all 16 functions that were
stripped actually need `external_body` restored since they either touch `static mut` or call these unsupported macros and arch types.
Now I need to check whether the shims themselves use any unsupported constructs.
ved
specs. So the real question is whether I can keep external_body minimal by body
-verifying the shims instead. Query shims might be provable with the bridge, but mutating shims that assert postc
onditions over a fixed phys_view() state are fundamentally unprovable—they'd need admit
() in the proof body. Since the Inner methods themselves require external_body due to uns
upported constructs, calling them from shim bodies is safe via their trusted contracts. So I could mark just
the 8 Inner methods plus init and instance as external_body, then body-verify the shims with admit() where needed,
rather than marking everything external_body and reverting the entire strip
But
comparing the two approaches: Option A restores external_body on all 16 methods (matching the original design), adds
the three new specs, and requires zero admits—it's clean and honest
about what can't be verified. Option B tries to minimize external_body by body-verifying shims with admits
